To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the Graal compiler can achieve speedups of 20x on typical Scala collection workloads compared with the standard HotSpot compiler and (2) these speedups are achieved by a combination of aggressive inlining and specialization of generic code.

(1) the Scala collections library is slow, (2) this slowness is due to high abstraction overheads, (3) these overheads can be widely eliminated by a sufficiently aggressive JIT, and (4) the Scala collections are still slow, even when the JIT is enabled.
(1) Scala collection combinators are slow and (2) a sufficiently aggressive JIT compilation can widely eliminate these overheads.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) What is the overhead of functional combinators and how can we eliminate it with aggressive JIT compilation?
making collection operations optimal with the help of aggressive JIT compilation.
the following questions: (i) How can we make Scala's collections perform well on typical workloads?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Scala collections are not that slow anymore.
the performance of Scala collections can be improved with a JIT compiler.
Graal is a very promising and competitive JIT compiler.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Scala compiler can be optimized to generate code that is as good as the code generated by the HotSpot C2 JIT compiler.
we have shown that it is possible to make Scala collections perform well on the JVM.
we can make Scala collections as efficient as Java collections, and even better in some cases, with the help of an aggressive JIT compiler.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the performance of a language is not limited by the language design, but rather by the quality of the underlying JIT compiler.
the performance of functional collection combinators can be improved by a JIT compiler.
a JIT compiler should be able to optimize away overheads of generic abstractions.
